title: Ordaining for a while
hookLine: in Thailand and Myanmar many young men ordain for weeks or months

cards: A nineteen-year-old in Bangkok works at a phone shop, plays football on Sundays, and has a girlfriend his mother likes.

One July he shaves his head and his eyebrows, puts on saffron robes, and joins the monks in the temple. Three months later he takes the robes off, goes back to the phone shop, and nobody thinks he failed.
His family thinks he did something beautiful. Ordaining for a while: ordinary in parts of the Theravada world, and surprising to anyone who has never seen it.

teach.b: In Thailand, Laos and Myanmar, a short stay in the robes has long been part of a young man's life. The Pali word for leaving home is pabbajja, going forth: the same word the texts use for the prince leaving the palace.
In Thailand the traditional season is the three months of the rains retreat, when monks stay in one place.
Traditionally a man ordains once, before marriage or after a parent dies, and the merit of it is offered to his parents, especially his mother. In Myanmar the custom starts younger.

Boys go forth as novices in a ceremony called shinbyu. First they're dressed as princes, in silk and makeup, sometimes carried on shoulders or led on a horse, re-enacting Siddhattha leaving the palace.

teach.h: SHINBYU: THE PRINCE BECOMES A NOVICE.
teach.b: Then the finery comes off, the head is shaved, and the little prince becomes a novice with a bowl. Some stay only a week or two.
What makes this possible is the monastic code itself: a monk may formally give back the training and return to lay life.
Leaving the robes is not a disgrace. The monastery is less a door that locks behind you, more a school you can attend for a season.
Some men say, years later, that those weeks changed how they eat, how they listen, how they speak to their parents. Now look back at the week. Two wings, calm and insight.
See clearly. Rising, falling. A map, not a scoreboard.
Entering the stream. Give and receive.

how: In Thailand many men ordain for the three-month rains retreat, often once in a lifetime; in Myanmar boys go forth as novices for a short time in a shinbyu ceremony, and leaving the robes afterward is accepted and honored.

a pilgrimage to the Buddha's birthplace

games.q: match the pieces of a short ordination.

games.q: you're twenty-two, in Thailand, and your mother asks whether you'll ordain for the rains before you marry. what does the custom expect?
o: become a monk for life, or not at all.
ordain for a season, then come home.
send money to the temple instead.
games.why: a season in robes is a long custom, and families often see it as a gift of merit to the parents; coming home afterward is part of the plan.

practice: Picture three months in robes, starting tomorrow: your phone in a drawer, your hair gone, eating what's put in your bowl and nothing after noon.

Walk through one ordinary morning like that, waking before dawn, the chanting, the barefoot walk down the road, and notice what you'd miss first and what you might not miss at all. Then let the picture go, and just breathe.

wordCard.voice: Pabbajja. Going forth from home: the word for a prince leaving the palace, and for the short ordinations many young men take for a while.

orig.note: Pali pabbajjā: going forth from home into homelessness; the word for the prince leaving the palace and for a novice's first ordination.

carryVoice: Your line: for a while. Not forever, and no failure in coming home. Week's end: day three hundred one.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga I (going forth and full ordination)
